claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is primarily governed by interfacial shear localization.
The interplay of severe lattice distortion and short-range order triggers interfacial shear localization.
Interfacial shear localization preferentially activates interface-mediated dislocation motion.
Twinning may also be activated at the interfaces.
Interface-mediated defect activity progressively degrades the structural integrity of the multilayer.
The proposed initial material consists of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The initial multilayer possesses severe lattice distortion and short-range order.
Sustained loading at an appropriate homologous temperature activates time-dependent plasticity mechanisms.
FCC/BCC interfaces are the critical sites of deformation activity.
Lattice distortion and compositional complexity localize stress at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Localized interfacial stress enhances dislocation activity and potentially twinning.
Progressive plastic deformation occurs through gradual defect accumulation and interface shear localization.
Sustained loading will increase dislocation density relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Plastic deformation under sustained loading will be localized preferentially at the interfaces.
Mechanical stiffness will decrease measurably over time under sustained loading.
The as-deposited multilayer has minimal dislocation density and a uniform structural state.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the multilayer architecture remains nanoscale.
The proposed mechanism applies in a creep regime where diffusion-mediated processes do not dominate.
Reducing layer thickness, and thereby increasing interface density, should correlate with increased localized dislocation density or interface-shear features.
Absence of both the predicted thickness-dependent interfacial deformation and progressive mechanical degradation would falsify the hypothesis.
